title: Plateau 120-degree cell-wall junctions and hexagonal packing
look_for_in_this_kingdom: leaf and root epidermis, shoot apical meristem, parenchyma and cork sections; segmented cell-network datasets (e.g. confocal meristem atlases)
variables_needed: neighbour counts or polygon-class distribution per cell

claims.label: Tissue cell walls meet three at a time at 120°, regardless of cell size
claims.statement: In sections of tissues such as plant parenchyma, as in a froth of soap-bubbles, cell walls meet three at a time at angles of 120° whatever the sizes of the cells, while the relative sizes of neighbouring cells determine only the curvature of the walls.
claims.quote: in both cases we see the cell-walls everywhere meeting, by threes, at angles of 120°, irrespective of the size of the individual cells: whose relative size, on the other hand, determines the _curvature_ of the partition-walls.

claims.label: Cylinders or spheres pressed into full surface contact form hexagons
claims.statement: Whenever cylinders or spheres of similar size are brought into complete surface contact by any uniform force (surface tension, growth pressure or external pressure), they tend to form a pattern of hexagons in section or surface view, each meeting six neighbours with 120° angles.
claims.quote: wherever we have a system of cylinders or spheres, associated together with sufficient mutual interaction to bring them into complete surface contact, there, in section or in surface view, we tend to get a pattern of hexagons.

other_kingdoms_hint.animals: epithelia (Drosophila wing disc and pupal wing, Hydra, cornea, retina), honeycomb and insect cells, ommatidia; neighbour-count (Lewis law) datasets; wing venation networks
other_kingdoms_hint.fossils: cellularly preserved tissue (Rhynie chert, fossil wood and cork, silicified plants), fossil bee comb or wasp nests, foraminifera or bryozoan packing
